questions.prompt: A general descent iteration updates the point by
questions.explanation: The iteration separates three choices: a descent direction, a positive step length, and a stopping test. The update that uses the first two is \(x^+ = x + t d\). Replacing \(x\) by the gradient changes the meaning of the vector. Leaving \(x\) fixed does not move. Adding a positive multiple of the gradient walks uphill.

options: \(x^+ = x + t d\) with a step length \(t > 0\) and a descent direction \(d\)
\(x^+ = \nabla f(x)\)
\(x^+ = x\) whenever the gradient is nonzero
\(x^+ = t\, \nabla f(x)\) with \(t > 0\)

questions.prompt: Take \(x = (2, 1)\), \(d = (-4, 2)\), and step length \(t = 1/2\). What is the squared Euclidean length of the displacement \(t d\)?
questions.explanation: The displacement is \((1/2)(-4, 2) = (-2, 1)\). Its squared length is \(4 + 1 = 5\). Equivalently, \(t^2 \lVert d\rVert^2 = (1/4)(16 + 4) = 5\). Reporting \(20\) is \(\lVert d\rVert^2\) before the step length. Reporting \(2\) is the absolute value of one component. Reporting \(\sqrt{5}\) is the length, not the squared length.

questions.prompt: A typical stopping test for this iteration is
questions.explanation: The direction is built so that the directional derivative is negative. That is an input to the step, not a reason to stop. Stopping looks at progress: a small gradient norm means the first-order model has nowhere useful to go. The step length is a positive real number. Replacing the objective by a constraint changes the problem.
questions.figure_alt: A curve that drops at first and then flattens.
options: the chosen direction fails \(\nabla f^T d < 0\)
the step length is required to be an integer
the objective is replaced by a constraint
the gradient norm is small

questions.prompt: Put one iteration in the order a descent method carries it out. Each step uses the result of the step before it.
questions.explanation: The gradient is the raw material for the direction, so it comes first. The step length is a distance along a direction that already exists. The update can be formed only after both are known, and the stopping test looks at the point that update produced. Testing for a stop before the gradient exists has nothing to measure. Choosing the step length before the direction does not define the ray.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 280 200" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>a segment in the first quadrant</title><line x1="40" y1="168" x2="250" y2="168"/><polygon points="250,168 243.6,170.7 243.6,165.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><line x1="48" y1="184" x2="48" y2="22"/><polygon points="48,22 50.7,28.4 45.3,28.4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="244" y="184" text-anchor="end" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x1</text><text x="56" y="18" text-anchor="start" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x2</text><line x1="188" y1="168" x2="48" y2="48" stroke-width="2.4"/><circle cx="188" cy="168" r="2.6" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="48" cy="48" r="2.6" fill="currentColor"/></svg>

steps: Compute the gradient at the current point.
Build a descent direction from that gradient.
Select a positive step length along the direction.
Replace the point by the point plus the step length times the direction.
Apply a stopping test, such as a small gradient norm at the new point.

questions.prompt: The gradient at the current point is nonzero. Which of these are legitimate descent directions for the iteration?
questions.explanation:
Each legitimate choice has a negative directional derivative.
• \(d = -
abla f\) gives \(-\lVert
abla fVert^2 < 0\).
• Newton with a positive definite Hessian gives \(-
abla f^T H^{-1} 
abla f < 0\).
• A positive definite scaling \(D\) gives \(-
abla f^T D 
abla f < 0\).
• \(d = 
abla f\) gives \(\lVert
abla fVert^2 > 0\), an ascent direction.
• The zero vector has directional derivative \(0\), so it is not a descent direction.

options: Steepest descent, \(d = -\nabla f(x)\).
The gradient itself, \(d = \nabla f(x)\).
A Newton direction \(d = -H^{-1} \nabla f(x)\) when the Hessian \(H\) is positive definite.
The zero vector.
A scaled direction \(d = -D \nabla f(x)\) with \(D\) symmetric positive definite.

questions.prompt: The current first coordinate is \(a\), the step length is \(t\), and the first component of the direction is \(b\). The next first coordinate equals
questions.explanation: The update is componentwise. The first coordinate of \(x + t d\) is \(a + t b\). All three names appear: the old coordinate, the step length, and the direction component. Subtracting \(t b\) walks against the direction. Replacing the product by a sum \(a + t + b\) adds quantities that do not share a meaning. Using \(a \cdot t\) drops the direction.

questions.prompt: A note takes one steepest-descent step from \(x = (4, 1)\) where \(\nabla f(x) = (2, -2)\). Exactly one step is a false claim.
questions.explanation: The gradient is given as \((2, -2)\). Steepest descent negates it, so \(d = (-2, 2)\). The directional derivative is \(2 \cdot (-2) + (-2) \cdot 2 = -8\). The false step adds the gradient instead of the steepest direction. The point \(x + 1 \cdot d\) is \((4, 1) + (-2, 2) = (2, 3)\), not \((6, -1)\).

steps: The gradient at the current point is \((2, -2)\).
Steepest descent uses the direction \(d = -\nabla f(x) = (-2, 2)\).
With step length \(1\), the next point is \((4, 1) + (2, -2) = (6, -1)\).
The directional derivative of this steepest direction is \(-8\), which is negative.
reasons: The update added the gradient. The steepest step adds the negative gradient.
Steepest descent should have used \(d = \nabla f(x)\).
The directional derivative of \(-\nabla f\) is positive here.

questions.prompt: A stopping rule looks at \(\nabla f(x) = (3, 4)\). What is the Euclidean norm of this gradient?
questions.explanation: The squared norm is \(9 + 16 = 25\), so the norm is \(5\). Reporting \(25\) stops at the square. Reporting \(7\) adds the components. Reporting \(12\) is their product. The test compares this norm with a tolerance. The value \(5\) is what gets compared.

questions.prompt: The Gauss-Newton direction and the Newton direction differ in what they invert:
questions.explanation: Newton builds \(d = -H_f(x)^{-1} \nabla f(x)\) from the Hessian of the objective. Gauss-Newton is aimed at a sum of squares. It linearizes the residual and inverts the Gram matrix of the residual Jacobian, which is the Hessian of the least-squares objective with the second-derivative term left out. Both directions still use the gradient. Steepest descent is the method that uses no matrix.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>a diagonal array</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">a   0</text><text x="98" y="86" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">0   b</text></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A two-by-two array with labels on the diagonal.
options: Gauss-Newton inverts the Hessian, while Newton uses the negative gradient with no matrix
neither uses the gradient
Gauss-Newton inverts a residual Gram matrix, while Newton inverts the Hessian of \(f\)
both invert the same Hessian of \(f\)

questions.prompt: On a smooth quadratic with a positive definite Hessian, the exact step length along a fixed direction is
questions.explanation: Restricting a quadratic to the line \(x + t d\) produces a parabola in the scalar \(t\). The exact step length is the \(t\) that minimizes that parabola. It equals 1 only for special directions, such as a pure Newton step on a quadratic. The reciprocal of the gradient norm is a different normalization. A quadratic is exactly the case where the line search has a closed form.

options: always equal to 1
the minimizer of the objective restricted to that line
the reciprocal of the gradient norm, for every direction
illegal, because a quadratic has no line search

questions.prompt: From \(x = (0, 5)\), take \(d = (-2, -1)\) and \(t = 3\). What is the squared Euclidean length of the displacement?
questions.explanation: The displacement is \(3(-2, -1) = (-6, -3)\). Its squared length is \(36 + 9 = 45\). Equivalently, \(t^2 \lVert d\rVert^2 = 9 \cdot 5 = 45\). Reporting \(5\) is \(\lVert d\rVert^2\). Reporting \(9\) is \(t^2\). Reporting \(-6\) is one component of the displacement, and the squared length is positive.

questions.prompt: A Gauss-Newton step fits into this framework as
questions.explanation: The framework keeps the update \(x^+ = x + t d\). Gauss-Newton supplies a particular \(d\), by solving a linear least-squares model of the residual. The step length is still free, and a stopping test is still applied. The condition number is not the step length. The objective stays a sum of squares.
